theme: Unit 16 review, The New Covenant Inaugurated, Luke
memoryText: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Jesus says this to the crowd that grumbled that he had gone to be the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus has just given half his goods to the poor, and Jesus replies with his own mission statement.

“For the Son of Man.” This is Jesus’ favorite title for himself. It comes from Daniel 7, the one who receives dominion from the Ancient of Days, and it also speaks of his humanity. He is the glorious King and the humble servant.

“Came.” He came on purpose. Salvation is not a rescue improvised in an emergency. The Son came from the Father with a mission, and Luke has shown it from the manger to the empty tomb.

“To seek.” God is the one who seeks. In Luke 15 the shepherd goes after the sheep, the woman searches for the coin, and the father watches the road. Christianity is not a story of humans reaching up for God but of God reaching down. Even our seeking is a response to being sought.

“And to save.” The seeking has a purpose, and the purpose is rescue. He came to give his life as a ransom, as he showed on the cross.

“The lost.” That is who he seeks. Not the confident or the righteous in their own eyes, but those who know they are lost, like Zacchaeus in his tree, the thief on the cross, the prodigal in the pigsty, and you.

When you feel too far gone, say this verse. You are exactly who he came for.
unitRecap: You have read the whole Gospel of Luke, and the thread running through it is that salvation is for everyone, including those the world overlooks. It opens with songs: Mary’s Magnificat, in which God lifts up the lowly and sends the rich away empty, and Zechariah’s Benedictus, which celebrates a God who keeps his covenant. The Savior is born in a manger, announced first to shepherds, and welcomed by Simeon and Anna as a light for the Gentiles. In Nazareth he reads Isaiah 61 and declares that the Scripture is fulfilled in him. He is filled with the Holy Spirit, and he prays at every turning point, before his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, on the mountain, and in the garden. He eats with sinners, honors a centurion’s faith, and forgives a woman who loves much. On the road to Jerusalem he teaches the parables found only in Luke: the Good Samaritan, the rich fool, the lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son, Lazarus, the Pharisee and the tax collector. He meets Zacchaeus and says that he came to seek and save the lost. In Jerusalem he institutes the new covenant in his blood, prays in Gethsemane, is betrayed and denied, declared innocent, and crucified. He forgives his killers, promises paradise to a thief, and commits his spirit to the Father. On the third day he rises and walks with two discouraged disciples, opening to them all the Scriptures concerning himself. The Gospel ends with the commission to preach repentance and forgiveness to all nations, and the promise of the Spirit. Along the way you also prayed Psalms 113, 116, 117, 27, 28, 31, 41, and 55, which gave words to the praise, trust, and betrayal in the story.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the Magnificat reveal about the kind of salvation God brings?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Reread Luke 1:46-55 and Psalm 113. Notice the reversal of the proud and the lowly, and the link to the promise made to Abraham. Write a few sentences about how this song sets the tone for the whole Gospel.

reviewQuestions.question: How does Luke emphasize the role of the Holy Spirit?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think of the Spirit’s presence at John’s birth, Mary’s conception, Jesus’ baptism, the wilderness, Nazareth, and the promise of the Father in chapter 24. What difference does the Spirit make in Jesus’ life, and what does he promise for his followers?

reviewQuestions.question: What does Luke’s emphasis on prayer teach us about Jesus’ own spiritual life?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Recall the times Jesus prayed: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, in desolate places, on the mountain, in Gethsemane, and on the cross. Pick one and describe what it shows about his dependence on the Father and what it means for your own prayer.

reviewQuestions.question: How does the road to Emmaus teach us how to read the whole Bible?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Reread Luke 24:25-27 and 24:44-47. Jesus says that Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms are about him. Name one Old Testament passage from this plan that you now read differently because of this, and explain how it points to Christ.

prayerPrompts: Thank God for sending his Son to seek and save the lost, and for finding you.
Tell him what you have seen in Jesus through Luke.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
